chunks: What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Abū Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī, who said:

I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: Nabīdh got onto my garment; may I perform salat (prayer) in it? He said, "Yes." I said: A drop of nabīdh dripped into a large jar from which I drink. He said, "Yes. Indeed, the basis of nabīdh is halal (permissible), whereas the basis of khamr is haram (forbidden)."

So the first point in it is that it is not apparent from the outward wording of the report that what touched him from the nabīdh was the intoxicating and forbidden kind, rather than nabīdh which is not intoxicating. Since it can bear both possibilities, we interpret it as nabīdh that does not intoxicate, and that is what we mentioned earlier: that in which small dates had been steeped so as to break the taste of the water.

key_terms.الْخَمْرِ: Wine or intoxicant whose origin is forbidden.
key_terms.حَلَالٌ: Permissible in origin and lawful to use.
key_terms.حُبٍّ: A large jar or vessel used for storing drink.
key_terms.نَبِيذٌ: A steeped drink; here understood in the non-intoxicating sense.

ai.seo_question: Can one pray in clothes touched by nabīdh, and what if a drop of nabīdh falls into a drinking vessel?
ai.summary: This report addresses the ruling of nabīdh in relation to garments and drinking vessels, indicating permissibility where the nabīdh is understood as non-intoxicating. The accompanying explanation clarifies that the hadith is to be understood as referring to nabīdh that does not intoxicate, distinguishing it from khamr, whose origin is forbidden.
